claim: Ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) damage causes steep discounting of future rewards (delay discounting [DD]).
source: Ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) damage causes steep discounting of future rewards (delay discounting [DD]) and impoverished episodic future thinking (EFT).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that motivates the study.

claim: Ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) damage causes impoverished episodic future thinking (EFT).
source: Ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC) damage causes steep discounting of future rewards (delay discounting [DD]) and impoverished episodic future thinking (EFT).
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known finding that motivates the study.

claim: DD was steeper in vmPFC patients compared to controls.
source: We found that DD was steeper in vmPFC patients compared to controls, and not modulated by reward magnitude.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the Results section.

claim: DD in vmPFC patients was not modulated by reward magnitude.
source: We found that DD was steeper in vmPFC patients compared to controls, and not modulated by reward magnitude.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the Results section.

claim: EFT cues downregulated DD in vmPFC patients.
source: However, EFT cues downregulated DD in vmPFC patients as well as controls.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the Results section.

claim: EFT cues downregulated DD in healthy controls.
source: However, EFT cues downregulated DD in vmPFC patients as well as controls.
evidence: This is a primary finding reported in the abstract and supported by statistical analysis in the Results section.

claim: vmPFC integrity is critical for the valuation of future rewards.
source: These findings indicate that vmPFC integrity is critical for the valuation of (future) rewards, but not to instill EFT in intertemporal choice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings stated in the abstract.

claim: vmPFC integrity is not necessary to instill EFT in intertemporal choice.
source: These findings indicate that vmPFC integrity is critical for the valuation of (future) rewards, but not to instill EFT in intertemporal choice.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings stated in the abstract.

claim: Human and non-human animals tend to prefer smaller-immediate over larger-delayed rewards.
source: Human and non-human animals tend to prefer smaller-immediate over larger-delayed rewards (Green and Myerson, 2004; Rudebeck et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Drug addiction is associated with steep DD.
source: Several clinical conditions, such as drug addiction and obesity, are associated with steep DD (Bickel et al., 2014), a disproportionate prioritization of immediate gratification associated with poor self-control and impulsivity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Obesity is associated with steep DD.
source: Several clinical conditions, such as drug addiction and obesity, are associated with steep DD (Bickel et al., 2014), a disproportionate prioritization of immediate gratification associated with poor self-control and impulsivity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Steep DD is associated with poor self-control and impulsivity.
source: Several clinical conditions, such as drug addiction and obesity, are associated with steep DD (Bickel et al., 2014), a disproportionate prioritization of immediate gratification associated with poor self-control and impulsivity.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Patients with damage to the vmPFC show abnormally steep DD.
source: Indeed, patients with damage to the vmPFC (Sellitto et al., 2010; Peters and D'Esposito, 2016; Lq et al., 2020; but see Fellows and Farah, 2005), and animals with lesions in homologous regions (Rudebeck et al., 2006), show abnormally steep DD.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Animals with lesions in regions homologous to vmPFC show abnormally steep DD.
source: Indeed, patients with damage to the vmPFC (Sellitto et al., 2010; Peters and D'Esposito, 2016; Lq et al., 2020; but see Fellows and Farah, 2005), and animals with lesions in homologous regions (Rudebeck et al., 2006), show abnormally steep DD.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: vmPFC is engaged in reward valuation and integrates different outcome attributes (e.g., amounts, delays).
source: According to a prominent model of intertemporal choice (Hare et al., 2009; Figner et al., 2010; Peters and Büchel, 2011), vmPFC is engaged in reward valuation and integrates different outcome attributes (e.g., amounts, delays), whereas lateral prefrontal cortex modulates vmPFC subjective value signals to promote self-control and future-oriented choice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research describing a model of intertemporal choice.

claim: Lateral prefrontal cortex modulates vmPFC subjective value signals to promote self-control and future-oriented choice.
source: According to a prominent model of intertemporal choice (Hare et al., 2009; Figner et al., 2010; Peters and Büchel, 2011), vmPFC is engaged in reward valuation and integrates different outcome attributes (e.g., amounts, delays), whereas lateral prefrontal cortex modulates vmPFC subjective value signals to promote self-control and future-oriented choice.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research describing a model of intertemporal choice.

claim: Cues to imagine personal future events during intertemporal choices reduce DD.
source: In separate work, Peters and Büchel, 2010 (see also Benoit et al., 2011) have shown that cues to imagine personal future events (episodic future thinking [EFT]; Suddendorf and Corballis, 1997; Atance and O'Neill, 2001) during intertemporal choices reduce DD, and the DD reduction relates to functional coupling of medial prefrontal regions and the hippocampus, and to the vividness of imagined events.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The DD reduction from EFT relates to functional coupling of medial prefrontal regions and the hippocampus.
source: In separate work, Peters and Büchel, 2010 (see also Benoit et al., 2011) have shown that cues to imagine personal future events (episodic future thinking [EFT]; Suddendorf and Corballis, 1997; Atance and O'Neill, 2001) during intertemporal choices reduce DD, and the DD reduction relates to functional coupling of medial prefrontal regions and the hippocampus, and to the vividness of imagined events.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The DD reduction from EFT relates to the vividness of imagined events.
source: In separate work, Peters and Büchel, 2010 (see also Benoit et al., 2011) have shown that cues to imagine personal future events (episodic future thinking [EFT]; Suddendorf and Corballis, 1997; Atance and O'Neill, 2001) during intertemporal choices reduce DD, and the DD reduction relates to functional coupling of medial prefrontal regions and the hippocampus, and to the vividness of imagined events.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: EFT effects on DD were not detected in amnesic patients with medial temporal lobe (MTL) lesions.
source: Indeed, EFT effects on DD were not (Palombo et al., 2015) or were inconsistently (Kwan et al., 2015) detected in amnesic patients with medial temporal lobe (MTL) lesions, in line with the evidence that MTL patients cannot imagine detail-rich future events (Race et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: EFT effects on DD were inconsistently detected in amnesic patients with medial temporal lobe (MTL) lesions.
source: Indeed, EFT effects on DD were not (Palombo et al., 2015) or were inconsistently (Kwan et al., 2015) detected in amnesic patients with medial temporal lobe (MTL) lesions, in line with the evidence that MTL patients cannot imagine detail-rich future events (Race et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: MTL patients cannot imagine detail-rich future events.
source: Indeed, EFT effects on DD were not (Palombo et al., 2015) or were inconsistently (Kwan et al., 2015) detected in amnesic patients with medial temporal lobe (MTL) lesions, in line with the evidence that MTL patients cannot imagine detail-rich future events (Race et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The vmPFC is a crucial substrate of prospection.
source: In addition to its role in reward valuation (Bartra et al., 2013), the vmPFC is also a crucial substrate of prospection (Schacter et al., 2012), and, accordingly, vmPFC patients are impaired in EFT (Bertossi et al., 2016a; Bertossi et al., 2016b; Bertossi et al., 2017; Verfaellie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: vmPFC patients are impaired in EFT.
source: In addition to its role in reward valuation (Bartra et al., 2013), the vmPFC is also a crucial substrate of prospection (Schacter et al., 2012), and, accordingly, vmPFC patients are impaired in EFT (Bertossi et al., 2016a; Bertossi et al., 2016b; Bertossi et al., 2017; Verfaellie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Constructed experience in hippocampal patients is mainly devoid of spatial references.
source: Whereas constructed experience in hippocampal patients is mainly devoid of spatial references, that of vmPFC patients also lacks relevant contents and sensory details, suggesting that vmPFC plays a more general (upstream) role in event construction (De Luca et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Constructed experience in vmPFC patients lacks relevant contents and sensory details.
source: Whereas constructed experience in hippocampal patients is mainly devoid of spatial references, that of vmPFC patients also lacks relevant contents and sensory details, suggesting that vmPFC plays a more general (upstream) role in event construction (De Luca et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: vmPFC plays a more general (upstream) role in event construction.
source: Whereas constructed experience in hippocampal patients is mainly devoid of spatial references, that of vmPFC patients also lacks relevant contents and sensory details, suggesting that vmPFC plays a more general (upstream) role in event construction (De Luca et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and represents an inference from the data.

claim: vmPFC initiates future event construction by activating schematic knowledge that drives the collection of relevant individual details.
source: McCormick et al., 2018, therefore, have proposed that vmPFC initiates (future) event construction by activating schematic knowledge (e.g., about the self, lifetime periods) that drives the collection of relevant individual details, which the hippocampus then assembles into spatially coherent scenes (see also Ciaramelli et al., 2019; D'Argembeau, 2020; Moscovitch et al., 2016; Ghosh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research proposing a model.

claim: The hippocampus assembles individual details into spatially coherent scenes.
source: McCormick et al., 2018, therefore, have proposed that vmPFC initiates (future) event construction by activating schematic knowledge (e.g., about the self, lifetime periods) that drives the collection of relevant individual details, which the hippocampus then assembles into spatially coherent scenes (see also Ciaramelli et al., 2019; D'Argembeau, 2020; Moscovitch et al., 2016; Ghosh et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research proposing a model.

claim: Twelve vmPFC patients and 41 healthy controls were matched in age.
source: Twelve vmPFC patients (see Figure 1 for the extent and overlap of vmPFC patients' lesions) and 41 healthy controls matched to patients in age (57.41 vs. 61.09; t51 = 1.61; p = 0.11), education (13.41 vs. 13.19; t51 = −0.22; p = 0.82), and gender balance (8 males, 35 males; χ2 = 2.12; p = 0.14) chose between smaller-immediate and larger-delayed rewards while we manipulated reward magnitude (small magnitude: €80/$100; large magnitude: €1500/$2000) and the availability of EFT cues during intertemporal choices.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison reported in the text.

claim: Twelve vmPFC patients and 41 healthy controls were matched in education.
source: Twelve vmPFC patients (see Figure 1 for the extent and overlap of vmPFC patients' lesions) and 41 healthy controls matched to patients in age (57.41 vs. 61.09; t51 = 1.61; p = 0.11), education (13.41 vs. 13.19; t51 = −0.22; p = 0.82), and gender balance (8 males, 35 males; χ2 = 2.12; p = 0.14) chose between smaller-immediate and larger-delayed rewards while we manipulated reward magnitude (small magnitude: €80/$100; large magnitude: €1500/$2000) and the availability of EFT cues during intertemporal choices.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison reported in the text.

claim: Twelve vmPFC patients and 41 healthy controls were matched in gender balance.
source: Twelve vmPFC patients (see Figure 1 for the extent and overlap of vmPFC patients' lesions) and 41 healthy controls matched to patients in age (57.41 vs. 61.09; t51 = 1.61; p = 0.11), education (13.41 vs. 13.19; t51 = −0.22; p = 0.82), and gender balance (8 males, 35 males; χ2 = 2.12; p = 0.14) chose between smaller-immediate and larger-delayed rewards while we manipulated reward magnitude (small magnitude: €80/$100; large magnitude: €1500/$2000) and the availability of EFT cues during intertemporal choices.
evidence: This is supported by statistical comparison reported in the text.

claim: Maximal overlap of vmPFC patients' lesions occurs in Brodmann areas 11, 10, and 32.
source: Maximal overlap occurs in Brodmann areas (BAs) 11, 10, and 32 of vmPFC.
evidence: This is stated in the figure caption and shown in Figure 1.

claim: People discount larger rewards less steeply than smaller rewards (magnitude effect).
source: A magnitude effect is consistently observed such that people discount larger rewards less steeply than smaller rewards (Green et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The magnitude effect has been ascribed to self-control mechanisms supported by the lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: This effect has been ascribed to self-control mechanisms supported by the lateral prefrontal cortex (e.g., Ballard et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: There was a significant effect of Reward magnitude on AuC.
source: An ANOVA on AuCs with Group (vmPFC patients, healthy controls), Condition (Standard, EFT), and Reward magnitude (small, large) as factors revealed an effect of Reward magnitude (F1,51 = 13.17, p = 0.0007, partial η2 = 0.20), qualified by a Group × Reward magnitude interaction (F1,51 = 9.49, p = 0.003, partial η2 = 0.16).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: There was a significant Group × Reward magnitude interaction on AuC.
source: An ANOVA on AuCs with Group (vmPFC patients, healthy controls), Condition (Standard, EFT), and Reward magnitude (small, large) as factors revealed an effect of Reward magnitude (F1,51 = 13.17, p = 0.0007, partial η2 = 0.20), qualified by a Group × Reward magnitude interaction (F1,51 = 9.49, p = 0.003, partial η2 = 0.16).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: Healthy controls discounted large rewards less steeply than small rewards.
source: Fisher post hoc tests showed that healthy controls discounted large rewards less steeply than small rewards (i.e., magnitude effect; p < 0.0001), whereas vmPFC patients discounted large and small rewards at similar rates (p = 0.76).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc tests.

claim: vmPFC patients discounted large and small rewards at similar rates.
source: Fisher post hoc tests showed that healthy controls discounted large rewards less steeply than small rewards (i.e., magnitude effect; p < 0.0001), whereas vmPFC patients discounted large and small rewards at similar rates (p = 0.76).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc tests.

claim: vmPFC patients showed steeper DD than controls for large rewards.
source: Relatedly, vmPFC patients showed steeper DD than controls for the large rewards (p = 0.04), but not for the small rewards (p = 0.67).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc tests.

claim: vmPFC patients did not show steeper DD than controls for small rewards.
source: Relatedly, vmPFC patients showed steeper DD than controls for the large rewards (p = 0.04), but not for the small rewards (p = 0.67).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc tests.

claim: There was a significant effect of Condition on AuC.
source: Crucially, there was a significant effect of Condition (F1,51 = 54.33, p < 0.0001, partial η2 = 0.52), indicating that both healthy controls and vmPFC patients had reduced DD rates in the EFT compared to the Standard condition (EFT effect).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: Both healthy controls and vmPFC patients had reduced DD rates in the EFT compared to the Standard condition.
source: Crucially, there was a significant effect of Condition (F1,51 = 54.33, p < 0.0001, partial η2 = 0.52), indicating that both healthy controls and vmPFC patients had reduced DD rates in the EFT compared to the Standard condition (EFT effect).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: The Group × Condition interaction was not significant.
source: In particular, the Group × Condition interaction was not significant (F1,51 = 2.18, p = 0.14, partial η2 = 0.04).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the ANOVA analysis.

claim: The Bayes factor for the EFT effect between vmPFC patients and controls represents anecdotal evidence in favor of the null hypothesis.
source: The results show a Bayes factor of 0.738. This value, which compares the likelihood of the alternative hypothesis to the likelihood of the null hypothesis given the present data, represents what Jeffreys, 1961 termed anecdotal evidence in favor of the null hypothesis.
evidence: This is a statistical result from Bayesian analysis.

claim: The Bayes factor for the group difference in the magnitude effect represents strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis.
source: It may be contrasted with the Bayes factor for the group difference in the magnitude effect (AuCLarge reward – AuCSmall reward, collapsing across the Standard and EFT condition; vmPFC patients: M = 0.01, SD = 0.10; controls: 0.14, SD = 0.13), which equals 11.52, representing strong evidence for the alternative hypothesis and against the null (Jeffreys, 1961).
evidence: This is a statistical result from Bayesian analysis.

claim: The magnitude effect was smaller in patients with damage confined to the vmPFC than in patients with additional damage to the lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: Note that the magnitude effect was even smaller in patients with damage confined to the vmPFC than in patients with additional damage to the lateral prefrontal cortex (−0.04 vs. 0.10; t(10) = −2.60; p = 0.03), confirming that the lack of a magnitude effect in vmPFC patients was not driven by damage extending beyond vmPFC (Figure 4).
evidence: This is a statistical result from a t-test comparing patient subgroups.

claim: In the Standard condition, the number of inconsistent preferences in vmPFC patients did not differ from that of healthy controls.
source: Post hoc tests indicated that whereas in the Standard condition the number of inconsistent preferences in vmPFC patients did not differ from that of healthy controls (0.75 vs. 0.94; p = 0.31), replicating previous findings (Sellitto et al., 2010), in the EFT condition vmPFC patients showed more inconsistent preferences than controls (1.12 vs. 0.61; p = 0.007).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc tests.

claim: In the EFT condition, vmPFC patients showed more inconsistent preferences than controls.
source: Post hoc tests indicated that whereas in the Standard condition the number of inconsistent preferences in vmPFC patients did not differ from that of healthy controls (0.75 vs. 0.94; p = 0.31), replicating previous findings (Sellitto et al., 2010), in the EFT condition vmPFC patients showed more inconsistent preferences than controls (1.12 vs. 0.61; p = 0.007).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc tests.

claim: The tendency to be more likely to choose the delayed option when decisions involve large rewards has been related to self-control mechanisms supported by the lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: The tendency to be more likely to choose the delayed option when decisions involve large rewards has been related to self-control mechanisms supported by the lateral prefrontal cortex. This region is more engaged during intertemporal choices between large than small rewards (Ballard et al., 2017), and transient disruption of its activity reduces the magnitude effect (Ballard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The lateral prefrontal cortex is more engaged during intertemporal choices between large than small rewards.
source: This region is more engaged during intertemporal choices between large than small rewards (Ballard et al., 2017), and transient disruption of its activity reduces the magnitude effect (Ballard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Transient disruption of lateral prefrontal cortex activity reduces the magnitude effect.
source: This region is more engaged during intertemporal choices between large than small rewards (Ballard et al., 2017), and transient disruption of its activity reduces the magnitude effect (Ballard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The absence of the magnitude effect in vmPFC patients points to the vmPFC as a crucial substrate of this effect.
source: Our finding that the magnitude effect is absent in vmPFC patients points to the vmPFC as another crucial substrate of this effect, and makes contact with previous evidence of impaired sensitivity to magnitude following vmPFC damage (Peters and D'Esposito, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the Discussion.

claim: Previous evidence shows impaired sensitivity to magnitude following vmPFC damage.
source: Our finding that the magnitude effect is absent in vmPFC patients points to the vmPFC as another crucial substrate of this effect, and makes contact with previous evidence of impaired sensitivity to magnitude following vmPFC damage (Peters and D'Esposito, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: An impaired reward valuation system impeded the differential assessment of the utility of large vs. small rewards in vmPFC patients.
source: We propose that an impaired reward valuation system impeded the (differential) assessment of the utility of large vs. small rewards, interfering with the normal triggering of self-control by the lateral prefrontal cortex for rewards of high perceived value (di Pellegrino et al., 2007; Ballard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings in the Discussion.

claim: Balanced intertemporal choice relies on vmPFC integrity and crosstalk with the lateral prefrontal cortex.
source: In the present study, steep DD in vmPFC patients was observed only on choice trials with large rewards, on which greater self-control (shallower discounting) was observed in controls than in patients, consistent with Peters and D'Esposito, 2016 view that balanced intertemporal choice relies on vmPFC integrity and crosstalk with the lateral prefrontal cortex.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and inference from the present findings.

claim: vmPFC integrity is not necessary to instill prospection in intertemporal choice with EFT cues.
source: This finding indicates that vmPFC integrity is not necessary to instill prospection in intertemporal choice with EFT cues.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the Discussion.

claim: In healthy individuals, EFT is thought to reduce DD by promoting self-projection into vivid future experiences, boosting the value of future payoffs.
source: In healthy individuals, EFT is thought to reduce DD by promoting self-projection into vivid future experiences, boosting the value of future payoffs (Boyer, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The EFT effect is not reliably observed in MTL patients.
source: As expected, the EFT effect is not reliably observed in MTL patients (Palombo et al., 2015; Kwan et al., 2015), who cannot imagine detail-rich future events (Race et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: vmPFC is thought to initiate endogenously the activation of high-level semantic structures.
source: In particular, vmPFC is thought to initiate endogenously the activation of high-level semantic structures (e.g., schemata; Irish and Piguet, 2013; Ghosh et al., 2014; McCormick et al., 2017; McCormick et al., 2018), for example, pertaining to the self, one's goals, common events (D'Argembeau and Mathy, 2011), around which the hippocampus then builds detail-rich future experiences (McCormick et al., 2018; D'Argembeau, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: vmPFC patients are particularly impaired at imagining self-related (as opposed to other-related) future events.
source: Indeed, vmPFC (but not MTL) patients are particularly impaired at imagining self-related (as opposed to other-related) future events, suggesting they fail to activate schematic self-knowledge that favors the collection of individual details for EFT (Verfaellie et al., 2019; D'Argembeau and Mathy, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: vmPFC activity drives activity in the hippocampus during both the initiation and elaboration of mental events.
source: Consistent with this idea, recent magnetoencephalography studies show synchronized engagement of vmPFC and the hippocampus during autobiographical memory retrieval and scene construction, with vmPFC activity driving activity in the hippocampus during both the initiation and elaboration of mental events (Barry et al., 2019; McCormick et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: vmPFC patients are not impaired in constructing future events if the task minimizes the need for self-initiation.
source: Similarly, vmPFC patients are not impaired in constructing future events (Kurczek et al., 2015; Verfaellie et al., 2019) or scenes (De Luca et al., 2019) if the task minimizes the need for self-initiation, whereas the deficit persists in MTL patients (Kurczek et al., 2015; McCormick et al., 2017; Verfaellie et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Subject-specific event cues acted as external triggers of self- and situation-relevant schemata, helping to circumvent vmPFC patients' EFT initiation problems.
source: We propose, therefore, that subject-specific event cues, which were self-relevant and familiar to the participants because they had been selected by participants themselves, and were already planned or were plausible in their future, acted as external triggers of self- and situation-relevant schemata, helping to circumvent vmPFC patients' EFT initiation problems.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings in the Discussion.

claim: vmPFC patients' intact MTLs allowed them to construct episodic future events, which were then integrated into intertemporal choice, reducing DD.
source: Their intact MTLs allowed them to construct episodic future events, which were then integrated into intertemporal choice, reducing DD.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the findings in the Discussion.

claim: The EFT effect on DD relates to the crosstalk between the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC, BA 32) and the hippocampus.
source: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) evidence has related the EFT effect on DD to the crosstalk between the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC, BA 32) and the hippocampus (Peters and Büchel, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The ACC is not necessary to update signal values with the EFT output.
source: Our findings suggest that the ACC is not necessary to update signal values with the EFT output, as this region was lesioned in our vmPFC patients.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the Discussion.

claim: In the EFT condition, subjective value computation relied on a more distributed network including the lateral parietal and posterior cingulate cortex.
source: Our findings are more compatible with the view that in the EFT (vs. Standard) condition, subjective value computation relied on a more distributed network including, in addition to the ACC, the lateral parietal and posterior cingulate cortex (Peters and Büchel, 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings in the Discussion, supported by a citation.

claim: The parietal cortex mediates shifts of attention to memories.
source: The parietal cortex mediates shifts of attention to memories (Cabeza et al., 2008) and across subjective time (Nyberg et al., 2010), and the posterior cingulate cortex is implicated in internally directed cognition and EFT (Schacter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The parietal cortex mediates shifts of attention across subjective time.
source: The parietal cortex mediates shifts of attention to memories (Cabeza et al., 2008) and across subjective time (Nyberg et al., 2010), and the posterior cingulate cortex is implicated in internally directed cognition and EFT (Schacter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The posterior cingulate cortex is implicated in internally directed cognition and EFT.
source: The parietal cortex mediates shifts of attention to memories (Cabeza et al., 2008) and across subjective time (Nyberg et al., 2010), and the posterior cingulate cortex is implicated in internally directed cognition and EFT (Schacter et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The lateral parietal and posterior cingulate cortex form a valuation sub-system dedicated to delayed rewards.
source: These regions were found to form a valuation sub-system dedicated to delayed rewards (Peters and Büchel, 2009), and may have updated reward value based on EFT, overcoming vmPFC patients' domain-general valuation impairment.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research and represents an interpretation of the findings.

claim: vmPFC patients failed at integrating optimally the attributes of choice options with the products of EFT.
source: One possibility is that vmPFC patients failed at integrating optimally the attributes of choice options with yet another aspect of the choice context, namely, the products of EFT.
evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the finding of increased inconsistent preferences in vmPFC patients in the EFT condition.

claim: vmPFC plays a role in weighting multiple aspects of choice options.
source: This interpretation is in line with the role of vmPFC in weighting multiple aspects of choice options (Pelletier and Fellows, 2019; Vaidya et al., 2018), and in synthetizing the emergent affective quality of a multi-element situation (Benoit et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: vmPFC plays a role in synthetizing the emergent affective quality of a multi-element situation.
source: This interpretation is in line with the role of vmPFC in weighting multiple aspects of choice options (Pelletier and Fellows, 2019; Vaidya et al., 2018), and in synthetizing the emergent affective quality of a multi-element situation (Benoit et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The lesions of vmPFC patients resulted from rupture of an aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery in 11 cases.
source: The lesions of vmPFC patients resulted from rupture of an aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery (in 11 cases) and from stroke of the anterior cerebral artery (in one case).
evidence: This is demographic information about the patient sample.

claim: The lesions of vmPFC patients resulted from stroke of the anterior cerebral artery in one case.
source: The lesions of vmPFC patients resulted from rupture of an aneurysm of the anterior communicating artery (in 11 cases) and from stroke of the anterior cerebral artery (in one case).
evidence: This is demographic information about the patient sample.

claim: Lesions were bilateral in 10 cases and left-lateralized in the remaining two cases.
source: Lesions were bilateral in 10 cases and left-lateralized in the remaining two cases.
evidence: This is demographic information about the patient sample.

claim: Four patients had minimal damage to the lateral prefrontal cortex (BAs 9, 46, 47), which constituted approximately 5% of their lesion volume.
source: Four patients had minimal damage to the lateral prefrontal cortex (BAs 9, 46, 47), but this constituted ~ 5% of their lesion volume, while their vmPFC lesions were on average 10 times larger.
evidence: This is demographic information about the patient sample.

claim: vmPFC lesions in patients with minimal lateral prefrontal cortex damage were on average 10 times larger than the lateral prefrontal cortex damage.
source: Four patients had minimal damage to the lateral prefrontal cortex (BAs 9, 46, 47), but this constituted ~ 5% of their lesion volume, while their vmPFC lesions were on average 10 times larger.
evidence: This is demographic information about the patient sample.

claim: Two patients had damage to visual cortex (BAs 17, 18, 19, 37) that constituted approximately 41% and 32% of their lesion volume.
source: Two patients had damage to visual cortex (BAs 17, 18, 19, 37) that constituted ~ 41% and ~ 32% of their lesion volume.
evidence: This is demographic information about the patient sample.

claim: The general cognitive functioning of vmPFC patients was preserved in all cases.
source: The general cognitive functioning of vmPFC patients was preserved in all cases.
evidence: This is a characterization of the patient sample based on neuropsychological testing.

claim: Long-term memory, as assessed with a list-learning task, was weak in 7 of the 12 vmPFC patients.
source: Patients' performance on standardized tests of executive function and short-term memory was also within the normal range in most cases (mean percentile > 5), whereas long-term memory, as assessed with a list-learning task, was weak in 7 of the 12 patients (see Table 1 for individual patients' neuropsychological data).
evidence: This is a characterization of the patient sample based on neuropsychological testing.

claim: Most vmPFC patients showed deficits in episodic remembering and EFT, as assessed with the Galton–Crovitz cue-word test.
source: Moreover, most vmPFC patients showed deficits in episodic remembering and EFT, as assessed with the Galton–Crovitz cue-word test, a long-standing method for eliciting autobiographical memories (Crovitz and Schiffman, 1974), later adapted to the assessment of EFT (Addis et al., 2008; see Appendix 1 for a detailed description of testing procedures in Italy and in Canada).
evidence: This is a characterization of the patient sample based on neuropsychological testing.

claim: Italian vmPFC patients produced fewer internal details than controls at the Galton-Crovitz task.
source: Post hoc Fisher tests showed that vmPFC patients produced fewer internal details (11.45 vs. 25.51; p = 0.004) but a similar number of external details than controls (11.39 vs. 11.96; p = 0.89).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc tests on the Italian sample.

claim: Italian vmPFC patients produced a similar number of external details as controls at the Galton-Crovitz task.
source: Post hoc Fisher tests showed that vmPFC patients produced fewer internal details (11.45 vs. 25.51; p = 0.004) but a similar number of external details than controls (11.39 vs. 11.96; p = 0.89).
evidence: This is a statistical result from post hoc tests on the Italian sample.

claim: Canadian vmPFC patients produced fewer internal details than controls at the Galton-Crovitz task.
source: The same ANOVA on the Canadian sample revealed an effect of Group (F1,22 = 17.76, p = 0.0003, partial η2 = 0.44), qualified by a significant Group × Detail interaction (F1,22 = 4.72, p = 0.04, partial η2 = 0.18), again indicating that vmPFC patients produced fewer internal details (10.63 vs. 31.78; p = 0.0003) but a similar number of external details than controls (16.79 vs. 25.65; p = 0.09).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA on the Canadian sample.

claim: Canadian vmPFC patients produced a similar number of external details as controls at the Galton-Crovitz task.
source: The same ANOVA on the Canadian sample revealed an effect of Group (F1,22 = 17.76, p = 0.0003, partial η2 = 0.44), qualified by a significant Group × Detail interaction (F1,22 = 4.72, p = 0.04, partial η2 = 0.18), again indicating that vmPFC patients produced fewer internal details (10.63 vs. 31.78; p = 0.0003) but a similar number of external details than controls (16.79 vs. 25.65; p = 0.09).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA on the Canadian sample.

claim: Subjective preferences were not equally well characterized by hyperbolic functions in the Standard and EFT conditions.
source: Preliminary fits of the hyperbolic function SV = 1/(1+kD), with SV = subjective value (expressed as a fraction of the delayed amount) and D = delay (in days), to individual participants' data using a nonlinear least-squares algorithm (implemented in Statistica Statsoft) revealed that subjective preferences were not equally well characterized by hyperbolic functions in the Standard and EFT conditions.
evidence: This is a result from preliminary analysis of the data.

claim: vmPFC patients' discounting curves in the EFT condition were not always monotonically decreasing.
source: This was especially apparent in vmPFC patients in the EFT condition whose discounting curves were not always monotonically decreasing (see Figure 3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for individual patients' discounting curves).
evidence: This is a result from preliminary analysis of the data, shown in figures.

claim: R2 values were lower in the EFT condition than in the Standard condition.
source: An ANOVA on R2 values with Group (vmPFC patients, healthy controls), Condition (Standard, EFT), and Reward magnitude (small, large) as factors confirmed a significant effect of Condition (F1,51 = 7.20, p = 0.009, partial η2 = 0.12) reflecting the fact that R2 values were lower in the EFT condition than in the Standard condition (0.54 vs. 0.64).
evidence: This is a statistical result from ANOVA on R2 values.

claim: The area under the curve (AuC) is a theoretically neutral, normalized measure of DD that does not depend on theoretical models regarding the shape of the discounting curve.
source: The degree to which participants discounted delayed rewards (DD rate), therefore, was measured using the area under the curve (AuC), a theoretically neutral, normalized measure of DD that does not depend on theoretical models regarding the shape of the discounting curve (Myerson et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a methodological statement supported by a citation.

claim: The AuC varies between 0 (maximally steep discounting) and 1 (no discounting).
source: The AuC varies between 0 (maximally steep discounting) and 1 (no discounting).
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the AuC measure.

claim: The smaller the AuC, the steeper the DD, and the more participants were inclined to choose smaller-immediate rewards over larger-delayed rewards.
source: The smaller the AuC, the steeper the DD, and the more participants were inclined to choose smaller-immediate rewards over larger-delayed rewards.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the interpretation of the AuC measure.

claim: Participants were presented with subject-specific cues to imagine personal events to occur at the delays associated with the larger-delayed rewards in the EFT condition.
source: In the EFT condition, participants were presented with subject-specific cues to imagine personal future events to occur at the delays associated with the larger-delayed rewards (see Figure 2 for an example trial).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: Participants identified planned or plausible personal future events for each of the seven delays in the discounting task in a preliminary session.
source: In a preliminary session, participants identified planned or plausible personal future events (e.g., appointments, anniversaries, outings) for each of the seven delays in the discounting task.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure.

claim: vmPFC patients had greater difficulty generating events in comparison to controls.
source: vmPFC patients had greater difficulty generating events in comparison to controls, and, therefore, all participants were allowed to refer to personal calendars and electronic devices, or to consult with their significant others.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental procedure.

claim: The Standard condition was run first to serve as the baseline.
source: The Standard, uncued version of the task provided a baseline for measuring the effect of future cueing on DD and was run first.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: The EFT condition was run at least 1 month after the Standard condition.
source: The EFT condition was run at least 1 month after the Standard condition.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Presenting the EFT condition first runs the risk of carryover effects of EFT into the Standard condition, leading to spurious DD baseline levels.
source: Presenting the EFT condition first runs the risk of carryover effects of EFT into the Standard condition, leading to spurious DD baseline levels.
evidence: This is a methodological justification for the experimental design.

claim: Studies have demonstrated the relative stability of individual discount rates over repeated testing.
source: Although the repeated-measures design we chose raises the possibility of practice effects, studies have demonstrated the relative stability of individual discount rates over repeated testing (Ohmura et al., 2006; Harrison and McKay, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.
